prompt: Your service averages 1700/s and its busiest hour runs at 2.5 times that. One app server of the size you are buying serves 500/s. How many do you need to stay at or under 80% utilization at peak?

options.whyWrong: This sizes the fleet to exactly meet the peak, which puts every server at 100% utilization. At 100% the latency curve has no finite value and load starts being turned away; the target exists to keep you off it.
This multiplies by the target instead of dividing by it, which asks for less capacity than the peak needs rather than more. Headroom makes the fleet bigger, never smaller.
This sizes for the weekly mean. The game resolves every week at its busiest hour, so a fleet sized for the mean is short by the whole peak multiplier exactly when it matters.

explanation: Peak load is 1700 × 2.5 = 4250/s. Capacity has to reach peak ÷ 0.8, and each server gives 500/s, so you divide and round up. Rounding down would leave the fleet over the target on the busiest hour.

prompt: An app server has a capacity of 400/s. Traffic averages 90/s and its busiest hour runs at 2.5 times that. What is the server's utilization at peak, as a percentage?

options.whyWrong: This measures the weekly mean against capacity. The game resolves every week at its busiest hour, so the figure that matters is the peak, which is higher by the whole peak multiplier.
This is the share of capacity still free, not the share in use. The two add up to 100%, and it is the used share that drives the latency curve.

This averages the utilization at the mean with the utilization at the peak. Nothing in the game runs at that average: the week is resolved at the peak, and a component sized for a blend is short when the busy hour arrives.

explanation: Peak load is 90 × 2.5 = 225/s, and utilization is received ÷ capacity at peak, so 225 ÷ 400. Every latency and error figure in the game is resolved at that busiest hour rather than at the mean.

prompt: A component has a service time of 10 ms and is running at 50% utilization at peak. What is its p99 at that load, to the nearest millisecond?

options.whyWrong: This is the mean response time, not the 99th percentile. Response times are spread exponentially around the mean, so p99 is about 4.6 times it.
This is the median, which is about 0.69 of the mean. Half of all requests beat it, so it says nothing about the tail the SLO is set on.
This is the service time on its own: what the component takes with nothing queued in front of the request. Under load a request also waits, and that wait is most of the figure.

explanation: Two steps. The mean is W = 10 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 20 ms, and p99 is W × ln 100 ≈ 4.605 W. Stopping at the mean understates what the slowest one in a hundred users waits by more than four times.
